title: Private equity value creation: where does AI pay in the 100-day plan?
description: A 100-day guide for the portfolio company COO. Which AI levers belong in the value creation plan, what each is worth and who owns it.
topic: AI in the private equity value creation plan
verdict: Returns now hinge on operating profit (EBITDA) growth, not cheap debt or rising multiples[^1][^2].
Lead with revenue: investors favour growth, and margin added almost nothing in the median buyout[^5][^4].
Price is the strongest single lever, yet only 14% of real plans change pricing[^9][^3].
AI drafts, ranks and flags; named people own targets, prices and credit calls[^8][^17].
Finish and measure: plans that complete more actions return more, so count dollars, not hours[^3][^7].

summary: AI speeds the analysis behind each move in a value creation plan, from pricing to collections[^8][^15]. The plan lists the moves that grow operating profit during a private equity hold, each with an owner[^23][^3]. Finishing makes or breaks it: plans that complete more of their actions earn higher returns[^3].
humanRole: Owner-CEO: owns the plan's targets and reports them to the board[^6]. Operating partners rate CEO ownership the top success factor, 4.6 out of 5[^6].
Commercial lead: sets price guardrails and approves quotes outside them[^8]. In a field study, AI price advice worked best when people priced the complex or unusual quotes[^8].
Sales leader: owns territories and account calls, while AI ranks accounts and drafts call plans[^12]. AI plus a human coach beat either one alone[^12].
Controller: owns credit holds, disputes and every number in the board pack[^22]. AI gets worse on tasks outside its strengths, so a named person checks it[^17].
teamAfter: Finance staff spend less time drafting: in one experiment, writing tasks took 37% less time[^14]. In one sponsored survey, 38% of sponsors put AI savings into strategic finance roles[^7].
Newer staff close the gap fastest: support agents with AI solved 15% more issues an hour, and the least experienced gained most[^13]. In sales coaching, middle-ranked reps gained most[^12].
Jobs change shape more than size: of US firms where AI changed tasks, 66% use it only to help staff[^18]. A national study found earnings and hours moved under 2%[^19].

example.input: Illustrative: a $50M-revenue distributor with 200 staff, in its first 100 days after a buyout. The inputs are 24 months of quotes and invoices, the open receivables ledger and 12 months of supplier invoices.
example.output: Days 1-30: a do-nothing baseline and a lever list sized in dollars[^23]. Days 31-60: pricing and collections pilots, each beside a holdout group that works without AI. Days 61-100: scale what beat its holdout, and report the dollar result to the board.

tables.title: Where do operating partners say delivery falls short?
tables.intro: EY, a consultancy, surveyed 120 operating partners in August and September 2026[^6]. Scores are out of 5.

recipes.name: 1. Revenue first: price guardrails and sales coverage
recipes.when: Most companies that sell on quotes. A point of price is worth more than a point off any cost[^9], yet only 14% of plans change pricing[^3].
flow: Controller: export 24 months of quotes and invoices by customer and product
Analyst with AI: find the price spread for like customers buying like products
AI: draft guardrail price bands for each customer group
Commercial lead: approve the bands and the override rules
Sales reps: price inside the bands, and give a reason code for each override
Sales leader: assign accounts from an AI ranking of fit and unsold products, with drafted call plans
Operating partner: compare margin each month against reps working without the tool
recipes.cost: Mostly your team's time, since the data already sits in your quote and invoice systems. Field studies saw about 11% more profit from price advice[^8].

recipes.name: 2. Cash and cost: collections and supplier spend
recipes.when: Companies with tight cash or large supplier spend. The evidence here is thin: one case study and one simulation[^15][^16].
flow: AI: rank open invoices by the risk of paying late
AI: draft reminder emails for the collector to edit and send
Controller: approve credit holds and settle disputes
AI: sort 12 months of supplier invoice lines into spend categories
Buyer: pick the top three categories to re-bid, and run the talks
Controller: track days sales outstanding (DSO) each week against the baseline
recipes.cost: Mostly team time plus any tool you buy. Each day of DSO is worth revenue divided by 365 in one-off cash (table below).

recipes.name: 3. Back office: month-end close and board pack
recipes.when: Finance teams whose close takes weeks. In one sponsored survey, 53% of companies with live AI agents use them to escalate variances[^7].
flow: Controller: list the close steps and who signs each one
AI: draft variance commentary and the first draft of the board pack
Finance lead: check every number and sign off
Controller: log close days and hours before and after
recipes.cost: Mostly setup and review time. In a writing experiment, AI cut task time 37%[^14].

ownData.title: What is one point of each lever worth at $25M, $50M and $100M revenue?
ownData.intro: One point of price is worth $500,000 a year at $50M revenue, about $3.5M of exit value at a 7.0x multiple[^9][^24]. A point off variable costs is worth about two-thirds as much; a point off fixed costs, under a fifth[^9]. We built this by plain arithmetic on 26 Nov 2026, from McKinsey's cost model and GF Data's average deal multiple[^9][^24].
rows: No volume lost, so all of it is profit
Kept at a 36.7% contribution margin (what each extra sale leaves after variable costs), implied by McKinsey's model[^9]
Variable costs at 63% of revenue, implied by McKinsey's model[^9]
Fixed costs at 18% of revenue, implied by McKinsey's model[^9]
Revenue divided by 365; one-off cash, so no multiple
ownData.note: Each cell shows the yearly profit gain, then exit value at GF Data's Q2 2026 average of 7.0x[^24]. The cost mix comes from McKinsey's finding that 1% of price, variable cost and fixed cost lift profit 6.0%, 3.8% and 1.1%[^9]. Limits: no lost volume is assumed, your own cost mix and multiple will differ, and McKinsey's 2026 update puts a price point at 8.7%[^10].

rules.name: FTC Act, as applied in Operation AI Comply
rules.what: The US Federal Trade Commission says there is no AI exemption from the laws on the books[^27]. What your AI tells customers is held to the same truth-in-advertising rules as your staff.

rules.name: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
rules.what: An airline was held liable for its chatbot's wrong answer to a customer[^21]. The tribunal rejected the idea that the bot was a separate entity[^21]. Any customer-facing AI in the plan needs a named owner.

rules.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
rules.what: It asks for clear human roles for oversight, written limits on acceptable performance and documented checks[^22]. Use it as the template for the owner map in your plan.

howToTest: Record a do-nothing baseline before day 1: 12 to 24 months of margin, DSO and spend, each with its source and date[^23].
Split the value bridge, which shows how much of the target comes from price, volume, cost and cash[^23].
Pick a holdout group: one site, product line, region or set of reps keeps working without the tool.
Write down the limits the AI must stay within, such as the lowest price it may suggest[^22].
Compare pilot and holdout each month in dollars: margin per order, DSO days, spend per unit.
Count hours saved too, but never alone. Only 38% of sponsors measure revenue or margin impact[^7].
Track the share of plan actions finished, since that share predicts returns[^3].
Report monthly to the operating partner and quarterly to the board. Scale only what beat its holdout.
watchOuts: Starting with the tool, not the problem: RAND lists the wrong problem and technology-first starts among the root causes of AI project failure[^20]. Pick the lever from the value bridge (the target split by price, volume, cost and cash) first.
Bad data at close: in one sponsored survey, only 6% of companies were data-ready at close[^7]. Spend the first 30 days on data.
No playbook: 41% of sponsors scale AI without one, by the same survey[^7]. Write the owner map before the first pilot.

Trusting AI outside its strengths: consultants using AI on a task beyond its reach were 19 points less likely to be right[^17]. A named person checks every number that reaches a customer or the board.
Hiding a sales bot: telling buyers about a bot cut purchases[^28], yet you are liable for what it says[^21]. Disclose it honestly and give it an owner.
Rosy price maths: the sizer below assumes no lost volume, which flatters price moves[^9]. Test price bands on a holdout before you book the gain.

faq.q: What is a value creation plan in private equity?
faq.a: A value creation plan is the list of moves meant to grow a company's value during the hold, each with an owner[^23][^3]. In 1,136 real plans, 84% included operational improvement and 74% top-line growth[^3].

faq.q: What is a 100-day plan in private equity?
faq.a: A 100-day plan is the first stretch of the value creation plan, where the baseline is set and the first moves start[^23]. Plans keep growing after it: 55% add operational items after year one[^3].

faq.q: What does an operating partner do?
faq.a: An operating partner helps portfolio companies deliver the value creation plan, working beside the CEO[^6]. When operating partners help shape the deal's core bet early, 68% of initiatives land, against 37% otherwise[^6].

faq.q: Where does AI fit in a value creation plan?
faq.a: AI fits inside each lever rather than as a lever of its own, speeding pricing, selling, collections and reporting[^8][^11]. Operating partners rate AI 3.8 out of 5 for priority but 3.1 for delivery[^6].

faq.q: Will AI shrink the team at a portfolio company?
faq.a: No, on current evidence: 66% of US firms where AI changed tasks use it only to help staff[^18]. Only 2% saw AI-related job losses[^18], and a national study found earnings and hours moved under 2%[^19].

faq.q: How do you measure AI impact in a portfolio company?
faq.a: Measure it in dollars against a do-nothing baseline and a holdout group, not in hours saved[^23][^7]. Only 38% of sponsors measure revenue or margin impact, while 67% count time saved[^7].

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy for standard work such as collections, spend sorting or close tooling: 76% of enterprise AI uses are now bought[^25]. Most companies lack a build team; only 9% of sponsors run an AI center of excellence[^7].
buyVsBuild.build: Build where your own data is the edge, such as quote history for price bands[^8]. Keep it small: one model on your own quotes, owned by your commercial lead and tested on a holdout[^8][^22].

pickElse: One lever only, such as supplier spend: start with the AI procurement guide or a spend analysis tool, not a full plan. Expect modest gains there[^16].
Just closed an add-on: start with the AI post-merger integration guide. Missing or messy data is a top reason AI projects fail[^20].
Month-end across several entities is the bottleneck: start with the multi-entity close guide. Weak data foundations sink AI projects before any lever pays[^20].
Sales coverage is the only gap: the lead scoring built into your customer relationship management (CRM) system may be enough[^25]. See the sales analytics guide.

answers.human-role: The owner-CEO owns the targets, and a named manager owns each lever: commercial lead for price, sales leader for coverage, controller for cash[^6][^8].
answers.team-after: Your team moves from building numbers to acting on them: checking exceptions, coaching reps and explaining results[^7][^13].
answers.example: A 100-day AI plan spends 30 days on a baseline and data, 30 on two tested pilots, and the last 40 scaling what worked[^23][^3].
answers.table-1: Pricing and selling have the strongest evidence. Working capital and procurement rest on one case study and one simulation[^8][^15][^16].
answers.table-2: AI shows the widest gap: operating partners score it 3.8 out of 5 as a priority but 3.1 for delivery[^6].
answers.recipes: Pick by your biggest gap: revenue first if prices vary, cash and cost if cash is tight, back office if the close drags[^9][^7].
answers.rules: No law governs the plan itself, but AI that talks to customers stays under consumer-protection law, and the US standards body NIST offers voluntary oversight guidance[^27][^22].
answers.benchmark: Set a do-nothing baseline, run each pilot beside a holdout group, and count the gap in dollars, not hours[^23][^7].
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI in the plan goes wrong when teams start with the tool, skip the data work, or trust output no one checks[^20][^7].
answers.buy-or-build: Buy for standard work like collections and spend sorting. Build only where your own data, such as quote history, is the edge[^25][^8].
answers.something-else: Pick something else when you need one lever, an add-on integration or a faster close, not a whole plan.

reviews.notes: Read as the portco COO who owns delivery. Owners are named per lever and the 100-day example gives the order of work. Jargon fixed: 'value bridge' now says it splits the target by price, volume, cost and cash; 'thesis' became 'the deal's core bet'; 'contribution margin' is glossed in the sizer.

Read on a phone for acronyms. EBITDA and DSO are spelled out on first use; CRM, B2B and NIST were not, and now are or were reworded. Every recipe step starts with the role doing it. The widest table has five columns, kept short by putting exit value in the same cell as profit.

Asked what it does to margin and whether one site can pilot. The sizer answers margin in dollars at three revenue sizes. The holdout step now names one site or product line as the pilot unit. No sourced pilot timeline beyond the 100-day split exists in the research, so none is added.

Read as controller and commercial lead. The collections and procurement evidence is labelled weak in the table and in recipe 2, with no vendor numbers padded in. The finance team-after bullet leaned on a writing study for a claim it did not make; it now states only what the study found. Price bands keep a reason code on every override.

Steve gets the answer fast: start with price, people own the calls, prove each lever against a holdout. His worries are covered: messy data (watch-outs), no proof (sizer plus holdout test), staff fears (FAQ, Census and NBER). No Zavient price is shown, by design. No change needed.
